questions.q: What is the actual nature of the gap that allowed Northfield's breach, as this case study frames it?
options: The SOC 2 auditor fabricated a clean opinion
A legacy API authenticated with a static key sat outside the asset inventory both audits sampled from, so it was never tested by either engagement
ISO 27001 does not require multi-factor authentication anywhere in its Annex A controls
Northfield never actually completed either audit
questions.explain: The legacy reconciliation API wasn't in the human-account inventory either audit's sample population was drawn from, so the MFA control both audits verified was never the control guarding that specific access path.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist that neither audit itself was a failure?
options: Because audits never actually test anything in practice
Because both firms were simply too reputable to have made an error
Because Northfield paid for a favorable outcome
Because both audits tested exactly what they were scoped to test, sampled correctly within that scope, and reported honestly -- the gap was in the organization's own asset inventory, not in the audit
questions.explain: A compliance audit tests the control environment as the organization itself has bounded it. It cannot discover an asset the organization's own inventory never listed.

questions.q: What does "compliance is a floor, not a ceiling" mean in the context of this case study?
options: Passing an audit confirms a necessary, real baseline, but it was never designed to be an exhaustive discovery process that finds every asset and access path in the organization
Compliance audits are a waste of time and should be skipped
A ceiling is a stricter standard than a floor, so organizations should aim for the ceiling instead of the floor
Floor and ceiling both refer to specific sections of the SOC 2 report
questions.explain: The audits verified a defined, scoped set of controls -- a genuine and hard-won baseline -- but were never built to discover every forgotten integration across the whole organization.

questions.q: What role did the third-party reconciliation vendor relationship play in this scenario?
options: The vendor's security was explicitly and correctly rated as outside Northfield's risk, with no further action needed
The vendor relationship is exactly the kind of ongoing third-party exposure Chapter 6 calls for continuous monitoring on, and a compromised laptop at that vendor was the actual entry point
The vendor had no access to any Northfield system at any point
The vendor performed the SOC 2 audit itself
questions.explain: A compromised laptop belonging to someone at the reconciliation vendor was how the static API key was obtained -- the exact kind of vendor risk Chapter 6 argued requires ongoing monitoring, not a one-time review.

questions.q: What kind of organizational practice is this lesson pointing toward as the real fix, beyond passing the next audit?
options: Hiring a different audit firm for the next engagement
Reducing the scope of future audits so fewer gaps can be found
Continuous asset discovery and periodic architecture review that looks at the whole system, not just the parts a specific audit's scope statement named
Removing MFA entirely since it didn't prevent this specific incident
questions.explain: The lesson points to the enterprise-wide, whole-system thinking this course has built toward -- continuous discovery and architecture review -- as what catches gaps that a scoped audit, by design, cannot.
